title: UML for interviews
scopeHtml: Scope: class, sequence, state, use-case and activity diagrams, mapping each to code, and how to draw them fast in an LLD interview. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why UML in interviews
notes.html:
UML is a shared drawing language for software. In an LLD interview you do not need the full standard; you need 5 quick sketches that show structure (class), behaviour over time (sequence), life of one object (state), who-uses-what (use-case) and workflow (activity).

The rule: draw the smallest diagram that answers the question. Interviewers judge clarity and speed, not UML purity. Plan on 2 minutes for a class diagram and 1 minute for a sequence diagram.

Worked example. Design a parking lot in 45 minutes: 3 min requirements, 2 min use-case list, 6 min class diagram, 3 min sequence for "park a car", 1 min state for a ticket, then 25 min code. Without drawing, candidates often spend 15 minutes confused about relationships.

Industry examples. Teams use PlantUML and Mermaid text diagrams in pull requests; Android docs show architecture as boxes and arrows; Uber and Netflix tech blogs use sequence-like flows. Few teams keep heavy UML tools, but all sketch.

Everyday analogy. A map, a recipe and a flowchart all describe the same city or meal from different angles. You pick the one that answers the question.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing everything at once. Ask "structure or flow?" and draw one.
  • Spending 10 minutes on notation details nobody asked for.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
A class diagram shows classes, their fields and methods, and how they relate. It is the main LLD artifact.

Box with 3 compartments: name, attributes, methods. Visibility: + public, - private, # protected.

Relationships, from weakest to strongest:

Association        A ------> B     A knows/uses B (field or parameter)
Dependency         A - - - > B     A uses B briefly (method parameter, local)
Aggregation        A <>----- B     A has B, B can live alone (Team has Players)
Composition        A <#>---- B     A owns B, B dies with A (House has Rooms)
Inheritance        A ------|> B    A is a B (extends)
Realization        A - - -|> B     A implements interface B
Multiplicity       1, 0..1, *, 1..*   on the line ends
+---------------------+          +--------------------+
| <<interface>>       |          | ParkingLot         |
| PricingStrategy     |          |--------------------|
|---------------------|          | -floors: List<Floor>|
| +cost(Ticket): Money|          | +park(Vehicle): Ticket|
+---------------------+          +--------------------+
        ^  (realizes)                    | 1
        |                                | owns  (composition)
+---------------------+                  v *
| HourlyPricing       |          +--------------------+
+---------------------+          | Floor              |
                                 +--------------------+
interface PricingStrategy { Money cost(Ticket t); }
class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy { public Money cost(Ticket t){ return new Money(0); } }
class ParkingLot { private final List<Floor> floors = new ArrayList<>(); Ticket park(Vehicle v){ return null; } }
interface PricingStrategy { fun cost(t: Ticket): Money }
class ParkingLot { private val floors = mutableListOf<Floor>(); fun park(v: Vehicle): Ticket = TODO() }

How it maps to code. Composition = field created and owned inside (new Floor() in the constructor). Aggregation = field passed in from outside. Realization = implements. Inheritance = extends.

Fast method. (1) Underline nouns in requirements = candidate classes. (2) Verbs = methods. (3) Add <<interface>> where behaviour varies. (4) Mark multiplicities. (5) Stop at 6 to 10 classes.

Worked example. "Library: members borrow books, max 5 books, fine after 14 days." Classes: Member, Book, Loan (association class holding dates), Library, FinePolicy. Member 1 --- * Loan * --- 1 Book.

Industry examples. Android Room entity relationships (one-to-many) and Kotlin domain models map directly to class diagrams.

Everyday analogy. A family tree plus an org chart: who is part of whom and who answers to whom.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up aggregation and composition. Say it by lifecycle: "does the part die with the whole?".
  • Arrows reversed on inheritance: the arrowhead points to the PARENT.
  • Showing getters and setters; skip them, show behaviour.

notes.title: Sequence diagram
notes.html:
A sequence diagram shows who calls whom, in what order, over time. Objects are columns, time goes down.

Elements: lifeline (vertical line), solid arrow (call), dashed arrow (return), alt box (if/else), loop box, opt box (optional).

Client      Controller     OrderService     PaymentGateway     Repo
  |  placeOrder() |              |                 |             |
  |-------------->|              |                 |             |
  |               | create(o)    |                 |             |
  |               |------------->|                 |             |
  |               |              | charge(card,500)|             |
  |               |              |---------------->|             |
  |               |              |      ok         |             |
  |               |              |<- - - - - - - - |             |
  |               |              | save(o)         |             |
  |               |              |------------------------------>|
  |               |    Order     |                 |             |
  |<- - - - - - - |<- - - - - - -|                 |             |
 alt [charge fails] -> OrderService returns Error, no save

How to draw fast. Pick the one scenario (happy path), list 4 to 5 participants left to right in call order, number the arrows 1 to n, add ONE alt box for the main failure.

Order place(Cart c) {              // matches the diagram above
    payment.charge(c.card(), c.total());
    return repo.save(new Order(c));
}

Worked example. Login with OTP: App -> AuthService: requestOtp; AuthService -> SmsProvider: send; AuthService -> Cache: store(otp, TTL 5 min); App -> AuthService: verify(otp); alt wrong OTP 3 times -> lock account for 15 min.

Industry examples. Stripe and Razorpay payment docs publish sequence diagrams of authorize and capture. OAuth 2.0 docs are sequence diagrams.

Everyday analogy. A script of a play: who speaks to whom, in order.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing every internal call; show only the calls that matter to the question.
  • Forgetting the return and failure path.
  • Mixing sync and async arrows (open arrowhead means async).

notes.title: State diagram
notes.html:
A state diagram shows the states one object can be in and which events move it between them. Use it whenever an entity has a lifecycle: order, ticket, vending machine, elevator, connection.

Parts: states (rounded boxes), transitions (event [guard] / action), start dot, end dot.

 (*) --> [Created] --pay--> [Paid] --ship--> [Shipped] --deliver--> [Delivered] --> (*)
            |                  |
          cancel             cancel [within 24h]
            v                  v
        [Cancelled] <----------+
enum OrderState {
    CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;
    boolean canGoTo(OrderState next) {
        return switch (this) {
            case CREATED -> next == PAID || next == CANCELLED;
            case PAID -> next == SHIPPED || next == CANCELLED;
            case SHIPPED -> next == DELIVERED;
            default -> false;
        };
    }
}
enum class OrderState {
    CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;
    fun canGoTo(n: OrderState) = when (this) {
        CREATED -> n == PAID || n == CANCELLED
        PAID -> n == SHIPPED || n == CANCELLED
        SHIPPED -> n == DELIVERED
        else -> false
    }
}

Code mapping. Simple: enum plus a canGoTo table. Rich behaviour per state: State pattern (interface State, one class per state). Big workflows: a state machine library.

Worked example. Vending machine: Idle -> (coin) HasMoney -> (select, stock>0) Dispensing -> Idle. Illegal moves (dispense with no money) are exactly the cells missing from the table, which also gives your test cases.

Industry examples. Order status in Swiggy/Zomato (placed, accepted, picked up, delivered), Stripe PaymentIntent states, TCP connection states, Android Activity lifecycle.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light or a parcel tracking page: only certain next steps are legal.

Common interview traps.

  • Missing the illegal transitions; say what happens on an unexpected event (ignore or throw).
  • Forgetting concurrency: two threads paying and cancelling at once need a lock or compare-and-set on the state.

notes.title: Use-case diagram
notes.html:
A use-case diagram shows who (actors) uses the system for what (use cases), nothing about how. It is the requirements picture, usually the first minute of an LLD interview.

Stick figures = actors, ovals = use cases, box = system boundary. <<include>> means always happens as part of another; <<extend>> means optional addition.

              +------------- ATM System -------------+
 Customer --> | (Withdraw cash) --<<include>>--> (Authenticate PIN) |
 Customer --> | (Check balance) --<<include>>--> (Authenticate PIN) |
 Customer --> | (Deposit)       <--<<extend>>--- (Print receipt)    |
 Bank staff-> | (Refill cash)                          |
              +----------------------------------------+

Fast method. List actors (human or external system) in 30 seconds, then 4 to 6 verbs per actor. Each use case later becomes a public method or a test case.

Worked example. Ride booking: Rider (request ride, cancel, rate), Driver (accept, start trip, end trip), Payment system (charge). Each oval becomes a service method such as requestRide(riderId, pickup, drop).

Industry examples. Product requirement docs at Uber/Ola start from user journeys; Agile user stories ("As a rider I want...") are textual use cases.

Everyday analogy. A menu that lists what each type of customer can order, without the recipe.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting implementation detail (database, classes) in a use-case diagram.
  • Confusing include and extend direction.
  • Forgetting external actors such as a payment gateway or scheduler.

notes.title: Activity diagram
notes.html:
An activity diagram is a flowchart for a process: steps, decisions, parallel branches. Use it for workflows such as checkout, refund approval or CI pipelines.

Symbols: filled dot start, rounded box action, diamond decision, thick bar fork/join (parallel), swimlanes (who does it).

(*) -> [Validate cart] -> <in stock?> --no--> [Show error] -> (end)
                              |yes
                              v
                 ===fork===> [Charge card]  ||  [Reserve stock] ===join===
                                              v
                                       [Send confirmation] -> (end)

Mapping to code. Decisions = if; fork = parallel calls (CompletableFuture.allOf / coroutines async); swimlanes = classes or services.

suspend fun checkout(c: Cart) = coroutineScope {
    val pay = async { gateway.charge(c) }
    val stock = async { inventory.reserve(c) }
    pay.await(); stock.await()
}

Worked example. Charge (800 ms) and reserve stock (300 ms) in parallel take about 800 ms instead of 1,100 ms in sequence, but now you must handle one succeeding and the other failing (compensate by refunding or releasing).

Everyday analogy. A recipe card with "while the pasta boils, make the sauce".

Common interview traps.

  • Using it where a sequence diagram (who calls whom) fits better.
  • Parallel steps with no failure or rollback story.

notes.title: Drawing fast in an interview
notes.html:
Order of drawing (about 6 minutes total)
1. Use-case list (text, 1 min)       -> scope
2. Class diagram (2 min)             -> nouns, interfaces, 1..* marks
3. Sequence of the main flow (1.5)   -> proves the classes work together
4. State diagram if an entity has a lifecycle (1)
5. Say what you skipped, then code

Tips that save time: use short names; skip getters/setters/types unless asked; draw interfaces first and mark them <<interface>>; number sequence arrows; write multiplicities only where they matter; ask "may I use Mermaid-like ASCII or boxes?" and keep the same notation throughout.

Mermaid (text) is often accepted on shared screens:
classDiagram
  ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" Floor
  PricingStrategy <|.. HourlyPricing

Worked example. At 5 minutes: 7 classes, 2 interfaces, one sequence. The interviewer interrupts to add "and discounts": you add a DiscountPolicy interface in 10 seconds because the diagram showed where the seam is.

Decision gravity. Diagrams are cheap and reversible; redrawing at minute 5 beats refactoring code at minute 35.

Everyday analogy. An architect's napkin sketch before the blueprint.

Common interview traps.

  • Perfecting the diagram and having no time to code.
  • Never connecting the diagram to code; always say which class implements which box.
  • Silent drawing; narrate your reasoning.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Five diagrams: class (structure), sequence (calls over time), state (lifecycle), use-case (who does what), activity (workflow).
  • Relationships: dependency < association < aggregation < composition; inheritance = extends (arrow to parent), realization = implements.
  • Ask "does the part die with the whole?" to choose composition vs aggregation.
  • State diagrams become an enum plus transition table; list illegal transitions as tests.
  • Draw order: use-cases, classes, one sequence, state if needed, then code.
  • Be quick, narrate, skip getters/setters, and link every box to code.
